sections.title: Foreword – Kashrut I
sections.html:
1

I thank God for granting me the merit of completing the first of the two parts of the laws of kashrut. The subject of kashrut is broad and complex. At first I thought to arrange the laws as they are arranged in the Shulḥan Arukh, in the Yoreh De'ah section, where the laws of kashrut are explained. That is, to begin with the laws of sheḥita (ritual slaughter) and tereifot, the prohibition of blood, ḥelev (forbidden fats), sheratzim (creeping creatures), meat and milk, mixtures, bishul akum (food cooked by gentiles), immersion of utensils and their kashering, and yayin nesekh (wine of libation) (SA YD 1-138), and afterward the mitzvot dependent on the Land and the laws of plants and animals (SA YD 292-333). However, out of a desire to explain the laws from their foundations, while studying the laws of sheḥita and tereifot, mixtures, and meat and milk, I found that if one wishes to look at the laws of kashrut in a complete manner, one must place the laws of plants before those of animals, since the main part of our food comes from plants: grain, legumes, fruits and vegetables. Therefore, the first part deals with the laws relating to the growing of plants, including the mitzvot of ḥadash, orla, kilei ilan and kilei behema (grafting of trees and crossbreeding of animals), kilei zera'im and kilei ha-kerem (mixed seeds and mixed seeds in a vineyard), and matnot aniyim (gifts to the poor) (chapters 1-6). After that, the permitting of plants for eating through the mitzvot of terumot and ma'asrot and ḥalla (chapters 7-12). Out of the engagement with plants, a chapter was devoted to the laws relating to the prohibition of 'bal tashḥit' (wasteful destruction), whose foundation is the preservation of fruit trees and foods (chapter 13). After completing the laws of plants, three chapters (14-16) were devoted to the basic attitude toward eating meat and the manner of raising animals, and within this an explanation of the general laws of tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim (causing suffering to animals) and shilu'aḥ ha-ken (sending away the mother bird). And another chapter (17) details the kosher and non-kosher species. And another two chapters (18-19) deal with the laws of sheḥita, the prohibition of 'oto ve-et beno' (slaughtering an animal and its offspring on the same day), kisui ha-dam (covering the blood), and the laws of the gifts that the Torah commanded to give from animals, such as the gifts from animals – the foreleg, the cheeks and the maw, firstborn animals, the animal tithe, and the first shearing. With this I have completed the first part of the laws of kashrut, which is called 'Produce and Animals' [lit. 'The Plant and the Animal']. In the second part I will explain, with God's help, the details of the laws relating to the eating itself: the inspection for tereifot – glatt and kosher, preparing food from animals by removing the blood and the ḥelev, meat and milk and the safeguards separating them, sheratzim and worms, the arrangements of the kitchen, the kashering of utensils, and the safeguards against bishul akum, yayin nesekh, and the immersion of utensils. Therefore its name will be 'Food and Kitchen'. It might seem at first glance that the second part should have been longer; however, as it appears now, it will be shorter than the first, since in terms of the number of mitzvot and laws, the first part is much larger and broader. Most of Seder Zera'im, which is one of the six orders of the Mishna that encompass the entire Oral Torah, is devoted to it, as well as several chapters in Tractate Ḥullin. Whereas the second part, which is indeed very practical, is the subject of most of Tractate Ḥullin, about half of Tractate Avoda Zara, and a little of Tractate Pesaḥim.

Some of the laws in this volume were explained briefly in Likkutim, part 1, chapters 12-13, and Likkutim, part 3, chapters 9-12. From now on they will no longer be printed in Likkutim.

2

The attitude toward the food that Israel eats in the Land of Israel is one of the expressions of a life of faith, as is expressed in the mitzva of the Torah to recite after eating Birkat Ha-mazon, whose essence is the blessing over the Land (Peninei Halakha, Berakhot 5:1; 5:4). For in the Land of Israel the holiness within nature is revealed (Orot Ha-teḥiya 28), and consequently food and eating are connected to holiness. In Birkat Ha-mazon we thank God for this, and in the system of mitzvot dependent on the Land we express the whole range of values that find expression in the food that Israel grows in the Land. First of all, in the mitzvot of ḥadash and orla: ḥadash in grain, and orla in the fruit of trees. These two mitzvot are meant to sanctify the first yield – in grain through the Omer offering to God each year, and in the fruit of trees through eating the fruits of the fourth year in holiness in Jerusalem. From these two mitzvot we also learn the foundation of self-restraint. Kilayim (forbidden mixtures) express the uniqueness of each species, a uniqueness that expresses the belief in Divine unity and its revelation in the world through a multiplicity of species, each species having a uniqueness of its own. In the mitzva of matnot aniyim we learn how to reveal the values of kindness at the time we merit to harvest the fruit of our toil. In terumot and ma'asrot and ḥalla, we learn how to fulfill the values of holiness and education in Israel, through the gifts to the kohanim and the Levites, and through Israel's eating of ma'aser sheni (the second tithe) in holiness in Jerusalem, while sharing the joy with the poor. Thus holiness is revealed within reality, and elevates the foods of the Land of Israel to the level of holiness, by whose power Israel receives strength and vitality to reveal the word of God in the world and thereby to repair it.

From this one can better understand that it is indeed fitting to open the laws of kashrut with the plants of the Land of Israel and with the fundamental laws relating to eating meat, through which the values that ought to be revealed in food are revealed, and from there to proceed to volume 2, which will deal with the prohibitions connected to food from animals and the safeguards against bishul akum. True, throughout the long exile, the central topic in the laws of kashrut was meat in milk and mixtures of meat and milk and other prohibitions, because we were occupied mainly with survival, whose halakhic expression is caution regarding prohibitions, as in the order of the laws in the Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah section. However, now that we merit the ingathering of the exiles and the building of the Land, it is fitting to return to the proper order, in which one can first express the values of holiness that are revealed through the mitzvot dependent on the Land. This follows the arrangement of the Mishna, which begins with Seder Zera'im, opening with the blessings over enjoyment and continuing with the mitzvot dependent on the Land.

Since most of the book deals with the mitzvot dependent on the Land, I devoted a long chapter (chapter 12) to a survey of all the mitzvot dependent on the Land throughout Jewish history, from the time Israel entered the Land in the days of Yehoshua bin Nun, through the destruction of the First Temple, the Second Temple and its destruction, until God in His great mercy granted us the merit to return to the Land and establish in it the State of Israel.

3

In the previous books I found it necessary to preface spiritual, faith-based introductions, sometimes in a chapter that opens the book, and sometimes at the opening of a chapter. Whereas in this book, which deals mainly with the mitzvot dependent on the Land, I found that there is no need for this; rather, the explanation of the mitzva is itself the idea, and there is no further need for any introductions. From here we may understand how deficient our lives are, for not all the exiles have yet been gathered in, and the Temple is still destroyed, and we cannot properly fulfill the mitzvot dependent on the Land and reveal the holiness within the entire expanse of concrete reality. Nevertheless, the fulfillment of these mitzvot according to the guidance of the Sages grants us inspiration and direction for revealing the values of holiness in the expanses of our lives, and through this, with God's help, we will speedily merit their complete fulfillment, and from the mitzvot connected to agriculture the guidance of the Torah will spread to the other professions.

4

It is a great privilege for me to thank my close partners in studying the topics: Rav Maor Kayam, shlita, a ram (Torah instructor) at Yeshivat Har Bracha, who accompanies me throughout all the study, and with his talent and diligence helps to clarify the topics; he rejoices in my explanations and novel insights and at the same time criticizes them meticulously, so that everything comes out properly clarified. Thanks also to Rav Efraim Shaḥor and Rav Yair Weitz, who helped clarify the topics, and they were recently joined by Rav Dani Keller. Rav Yair Weitz made a special contribution in clarifying the mitzvot dependent on the Land from the days of Yehoshua bin Nun until our own day, and in the safeguards of kilayim. And Rav Efraim Shaḥor made a special contribution in clarifying the topics of orla and other topics. I also thank Maor Horowitz for his participation in the study, for the content and language editing, and for arranging the book for printing. Thanks to Rav Yonadav Zar for the precise proofreading and the encouragement, and thanks also to my good and longtime friend, the all-round scholar Rav Ze'ev Sultanovitch, who clarified the general topics with me. And thanks also to Rav Uriel Shalmoni for his help in clarifying the topics and in proofreading.

5

It is a pleasant duty to mention with praise the books composed in the last generation that contributed to clarifying the topics. First and foremost, the 'Torah Ve-ha'aretz Institute' and its head, Rav Yehuda Amiḥai, for all the institute's many publications. I was also helped by the book of the institute's president, Rav Yaakov Ariel, shlita, 'Be-ohala Shel Torah', and by the important works and articles on terumot and ma'asrot of his son, my friend since youth, Rav Azriel Ariel, shlita. Of course, I was also helped by the responsa of my teacher Rav Shaul Yisraeli, ztz"l, on all the mitzvot dependent on the Land. I was also helped by the rulings of my teacher, the Rishon Le-Tziyon Rav Mordechai Eliyahu, ztz"l. I will also mention with praise the 'Mishpetei Eretz' books of the 'Beit Midrash Gavoha Le-halakha Ba-hityashvut Ha-ḥakla'it' (Advanced Institute for Halakha in Agricultural Settlement), which were written in a systematic and precise manner, and express mainly the approach of the Lithuanian poskim, headed by the Ḥazon Ish and Rav Elyashiv. It is also fitting to mention with praise the Derekh Emuna commentary on the Rambam's Seder Zera'im by Rav Ḥayim Kanievsky, shlita, which lays out with great erudition the opinions of the Rishonim and Aḥaronim and of his uncle the Ḥazon Ish. It is also fitting to mention with praise the books of Rav Shneur Zalman Revaḥ and the books of Rav David Tehrani. Also the commentary and notes in the wonderful series of the Talmud Yerushalmi in the Schottenstein edition on Seder Zera'im contributed much to clarifying the topics.

6

Thanks to my father and teacher, Rav Zalman Baruch Melamed, shlita, head of Yeshivat Beit El, and to my mother and teacher, from whom all the foundations of my Torah and outlook derive. Also special thanks to Inbal, my dear wife, who devotes all her strength to magnifying and glorifying the Torah, to the success of the study, and to the publishing of the books for the merit of the public. May it be His will that we merit to see all our sons and daughters, grandsons and granddaughters, rising in Torah study and the fulfillment of the mitzvot, establishing good and splendid families, and increasing truth, kindness and peace forever.

I would further like to thank all those engaged in the holy work of building the yeshiva and printing the books: R. Yaakov Weinberger, director of the yeshiva; Yoni Bozaglo, who is in charge of printing and marketing the books; Hadas Pedinker, who is in charge of printing and distribution; and to their predecessors in the management of the yeshiva and the printing of the books, R. Yaakov Katz, R. Dudu Sa'ada, Yisrael Sa'adya, Shalev Kayam, Ḥayim Margolis and Keren Fogel. May it be the will of God, may He be blessed, to grant all those who help and assist in the work understanding and strength to succeed in their work, and may they merit to establish splendid families, and may God fulfill all the wishes of their hearts for good.

Eliezer Melamed

Iyar 5778

sections.title: Foreword
sections.html:
1

I thank God for helping me and granting me the merit to complete part 2 of the laws of kashrut, and thereby to complete the laws of kashrut. The mitzva of kashrut elevates our eating, so that in addition to the health of the body it will also be directed toward the refinement of the nefesh, the ruaḥ and the neshama. As is the way of the world, spiritual people tend to belittle eating, and regard it as an inferior bodily matter that prevents a person from spiritual attainments, and therefore in their view there is no value in dealing with foods and eating them. However, according to the faith of Israel and the guidance of the Torah, everything is important, and there is holiness in the body as well, and therefore many mitzvot deal with directing the body and eating. Moreover, there is a deep connection between the body and the soul, and every rectification in the body affects the soul. The main aim of the mitzvot of kashrut is to make our food fit and pure, so that through it we can connect to the values of the Torah. Happy are we, how good is our portion and how pleasant our lot, that He sanctified us with His mitzvot and commanded us to elevate our eating to an eating that has in it faith, holiness and blessing, through which we can fulfill our destiny to repair the world under the kingdom of the Almighty.

2

In many respects this book was the most complex and complicated. It deals with the topics most frequently brought before rabbis throughout the generations, and consequently many books were composed and many responsa written about them. The commentaries on the Shulḥan Arukh are also especially numerous in these areas. On almost every chapter of this book, entire books were composed in recent generations. As in all the previous books in the 'Peninei Halakha' series, my aim was to define the foundations of the halakha well, so that the details branching out from them will be understood on their own, in such a way that there will be no need to pile up details and examples.

The principle that stands before my eyes is that the mitzvot of the Torah must be understandable to all of Israel, in such a way that every Jew can fulfill them without entering into doubts and constantly needing to ask a sage a question, which is meant for rare cases. For if people always need to ask about everything, only a few will observe the halakha properly. If this is so in the entire Torah, all the more so in a practical, everyday area that touches every family and every person. Beyond that, knowledge of the Torah elevates and grants inspiration to every person in Israel, so that he can bring his talents fully to realization in all areas of his occupations, for the glory of the Torah, the people and the Land. Therefore God gave His Torah to all of His people Israel, so that the words of the Torah would be known to all and not rest with the scholars alone. And only in this way can the people of Israel realize its destiny to reveal the word of God in the world and to be a blessing to all the families of the earth.

3

In several areas there was a need to delve again into the foundations of the topics, either because reality has changed, or because at times the poskim of previous generations related mainly to the traditions of their own locale and to the opinions of the rabbis of their own community, and less to the traditions and poskim of different communities and of distant places. Now that we have merited the ingathering of millions of Jews from the four corners of the earth, and the tribes intermarry with one another, we are obligated to study the customs of all the communities and the poskim together, to determine the halakhic foundation common to all of them, and, while preserving the different traditions, to strive to bring the halakhic branches closer to one another, in the way of the Torah scholars of the Land of Israel who are pleasant to one another in halakha (Sanhedrin 24a).

By the kindness of God, over the years outstanding Torah scholars have grown up in Yeshivat Har Bracha, who know how to clarify a tradition from its foundation to the spreading of all its branches in recent generations. It is a great privilege for me to thank my close partners in studying the topics, headed by Rav Maor Kayam, shlita, head of the institute attached to Yeshivat Har Bracha, who accompanies me throughout all the study. Thanks to his special talent and diligence, together with his deep understanding of the ways of halakha and its writing, his help in clarifying the topics is enormous. As head of the institute he taught and guided the members of the institute so that they too could help clarify the topics. In the laws of kashrut, beginning with the first part, their great contribution has already found expression. Thanks to them it was possible to encompass and clarify intricate topics while taking into account all the hundreds of commentaries and responsa that dealt with them, especially in the topics of sheratzim and the kashering of utensils.

Each of the members of the institute participated in a thorough proofreading of the entire book and in a general contribution to all the topics; beyond that, each one studied certain topics thoroughly. In particular I will mention the contribution of Rav Yair Dov Weitz in the chapters on bishul akum and the food industry, the contribution of Rav Efraim Shaḥor in clarifying the laws of yayin nesekh and roasting, the contribution of Rav Dani Keller in the topics that connect Torah and science, and the contribution of Rav Aharon Friedman, who recently joined, in the topic of supervision and reliability.

Thanks to Rav Eyal Moshe, a ram at the yeshiva, who has specialized for several years in kashrut and supervision, and helped with various topics. I also thank Maor Horowitz for the content and language editing and for arranging the book for printing. He is continually rising in the wisdom of language; and indeed, when the rules of grammar impair understanding, I prefer understanding. Many times, with his guidance, I found the way to unite understanding and grammar. Thanks to Rav Yonadav Zar for the precise proofreading, and thanks also to my good and longtime friend, the all-round scholar Rav Ze'ev Sultanovitch, who clarified the general topics with me. And thanks also to R. Netanel Rosenstein for his devotion in writing the index.

4

Very many books have been written on these topics, especially in everything connected to the laws of mixtures. It is a pleasant duty to mention with praise several books composed in the last generation that contributed to clarifying the topics: 'Badei Ha-shulḥan' on SA YD, the laws of meat and milk and mixtures, by Rav Shraga Feivel Cohen, and 'Ḥelkat Binyamin' on simanim 112-122, by his son who continues his work; the Shulḥan Arukh Ha-mevu'ar published by 'Oz Ve-hadar' on the laws of meat and milk; the 'Hora'a Berura' books from the beit midrash of Rav Meir Mazuz, which are precise and place emphasis on the poskim of Sephardic origin, from the East and the West. I will also mention with praise Rav Dr. Yisrael Meir Levinger for his books on matters of the kashrut of meat, the book 'Ekhol Be-simḥa' by Rav Moshe Bigel, 'Ve-akhalta Ve-savata' by Rav Elyashiv Knohl, ztz"l, the books of Rav David Tehrani, the books of Rav Amram Edrei, and the book 'Shemirat Ha-guf Ve-ha-nefesh' by Rav Yosef Lerner.

5

Special thanks to the residents of Har Bracha. Thanks to them I am familiar with all the practical questions from every area of kashrut. In addition, in the regular classes that I give every Shabbat for men and women, hundreds of listeners studied with me all the topics of kashrut, heard the questions and doubts, and contributed important reasoning and information. Even the fathers and mothers who visit the community and participate in the classes contributed from their experience and from the tradition of their fathers and mothers according to their different communities. Also, over the years, scientists and experts in various fields of knowledge have grown out of the yeshiva and the 'Shiluvim' program and have made their contribution to the book. So too from the responses of the readers of my 'Revivim' column, especially from the contribution of experts in the various fields of science, who added important information for understanding the topics and the reality.

6

Thanks to my father and teacher, Rav Zalman Baruch Melamed, shlita, head of Yeshivat Beit El, and to my mother and teacher, from whom all the foundations of my Torah and outlook derive. Also special thanks to Inbal, my dear wife, who devotes all her strength to magnifying and glorifying the Torah, to the success of the study, and to the publishing of the books for the merit of the public, and all this together with the devoted care of our large family. May it be His will that we merit to see all our sons and daughters, grandsons and granddaughters, rising in Torah study and in the fulfillment of the mitzvot, establishing good and splendid families, and increasing truth, kindness and peace forever.

I would further like to thank all those engaged in the holy work of building the yeshiva and printing the books: R. Yaakov Weinberger, director of the yeshiva; Yoni Bozaglo, who is in charge of printing and marketing the books; Hadas Pedinker, who is in charge of printing and distribution; and to their predecessors in the management of the yeshiva and the printing of the books: R. Yaakov Katz, Dudu Sa'ada, Yisrael Sa'adya, Shalev Kayam, Ḥayim Margolis and Keren Fogel. May it be the will of God, may He be blessed, to grant all those who help and assist in the work understanding and strength to succeed in their work, and may they merit to establish splendid families, and may God fulfill all the wishes of their hearts for good.

*

This book is dedicated to the elevation of the soul of my beloved cousin Tzur Hartuv, z"l, who passed away suddenly in the darkness of the night of the 16th of Tevet 5779, at the age of fifty-eight. He left behind his widow Yehudit and their five children. Tzuri, who was born in Bnei Brak and made his home in Efrat, was a graduate of the yeshivot Or Etzion, Merkaz Ha-rav and Har Etzion. He was devoted to his work in the field of insurance, beloved by his friends, among the volunteers in the community, set fixed times for Torah, and like his father, may he live, served as ḥazan on Shabbatot and the High Holidays. He loved Ḥasidic and Israeli music, accompanied weddings and sing-along evenings with his playing on the organ, and made himself pleasing to God with his voice and his deeds. Tzuri was the first to encourage me to write the laws of kashrut, emphasizing that the general public, and even yeshiva graduates, do not properly understand the complex topics of kashrut. At almost every meeting between us, and after the publication of each book, he noted that he was still waiting for the laws of kashrut. When the first part came out, he said that this was indeed a beginning, but he was still waiting for the clarification of the main topics. To our great sorrow, now that the book is being published, all that is in our power is to dedicate it to his memory. May his soul be bound up in the bond of life, and may he continue to serve as an emissary of the congregation in his prayer for all the members of his family and for Israel.

Eliezer Melamed

Marḥeshvan 5780
